options: A hosted copy of a repository on GitHub
A saved snapshot of a specific set of changes, with a message describing what changed and why
An isolated line of work split off from the main codebase
A request to merge one branch into another
questions.explain: A commit is a saved snapshot of changes with a descriptive message — a repo's history is just a chain of commits, one after another.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is a "branch" for?
options: A backup copy of the entire repository stored on a different computer
The specific commit message format a team agrees to use
An isolated line of work, so changes in progress don't affect anyone else until they're deliberately merged back in
A file that lists which files Git should never track
questions.explain: A branch lets someone work on a change in isolation, without affecting the main codebase, until it's deliberately merged back in.

questions.q: Where does a pull request fit into the everyday workflow this lesson describes?
options: Before any code is written, to plan out the change
It replaces the need for commits entirely
It only applies to the very first commit in a repository's history
After a branch is pushed to the remote, as a request to merge it — reviewed by a teammate before it's accepted
questions.explain: A pull request is opened after pushing a branch, asking for the change to be merged — and it's exactly the Code Review step from Lesson 4's Dev-stage diagram.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a commit message like "fixed stuff" is a problem?
options: Git will reject commit messages shorter than one sentence
It's technically a valid commit message, but it tells the next person reading the history nothing about what changed or why
Short commit messages make a repository load more slowly
It's not a problem — commit message content doesn't matter at all
questions.explain: A commit message should say what changed and, where it isn't obvious, why — "fixed stuff" leaves the next reader (including your future self) with no useful information.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about committing a password or API key into a repository?
options: It's safe as long as the file is deleted in the very next commit
.gitignore automatically removes secrets from past commits once added
Git automatically encrypts any file that looks like a credential
It stays recoverable from the repo's history forever, even after the file is "deleted" in a later commit
questions.explain: A .gitignore file only stops a file from being tracked going forward — it does nothing to remove something already committed, which stays recoverable from the repo's history indefinitely.
